description_ru: Страстная защита публичных библиотек как общественного пространства, равного доступа к знаниям и последнего места, где ничего не нужно покупать.
text:
Every few years, someone in authority discovers that the local library is a drain on the budget. The argument is always delivered with a sorrowful air, as though the speaker takes no pleasure in it. Books, we are told, are yesterday's technology; everything is now available online; and the building, with its heating bills and its patient staff, occupies valuable land that could house something more profitable. I have heard this case made in council chambers and newspaper columns, and each time I have found it both perfectly logical and entirely mistaken.

Let me begin with what is true. Fewer people borrow books than once did, and anybody who claims otherwise is not paying attention to the figures. A great deal of information, from train times to tax forms, can be found on a telephone in seconds. If a library existed merely to store printed paper and lend it out, the sceptics would have a decent case, and I would probably be among them. But a library has never really been a warehouse for books, any more than a hospital is a warehouse for beds.

What a public library provides is something that has become rarer with every passing decade: a space in which you are welcome without being a customer. Consider how few such places remain. A cafe expects you to buy a coffee within an hour or so. A shopping centre tolerates you as long as you spend money, and a park, however lovely, offers no shelter from the rain. The library is the last warm, dry, well-lit room where nobody will ask what you intend to purchase, and this simple fact has consequences that are difficult to measure and impossible to replace.

I saw those consequences one wet Tuesday morning last winter. In a corner sat an elderly man in a worn overcoat who, I later learned, had lost his wife that spring and found the silence of his flat unbearable. At the next table a teenager was doing homework because her family's house was crowded and noisy. Near the window, a young father was working through a job application on one of the public computers, with the librarian leaning over his shoulder to explain how to attach a document. In the children's area a volunteer was reading aloud to a handful of toddlers in four different languages. Nobody in that room was a customer, and nobody was a burden. Every one of them was a citizen using a public service exactly as it was intended.

It is here that the claim that "everything is online" collapses. It is true only for those with a reliable connection, a decent device and the confidence to use it. Millions of people in this country lack at least one of the three, and the number of essential services that now require an online form grows every year, whether it is claiming benefits, renewing a licence or applying for work. The library is where these people turn, and the staff who help them are performing a kind of social work for which they are neither trained nor paid adequately. If the building closes, the problem will not vanish. It will simply move, at greater expense, to hospitals, housing offices and emergency services.

I want to dwell on that point about cost, because it is the argument that campaigners tend to neglect. Economists who have attempted to measure the return on library spending have generally found that every pound invested yields several in benefits, from improved literacy to job-seeking support and reduced loneliness. Such calculations are inevitably rough, and I would not stake my life on the precise multiple. But the direction is not in doubt. Closing a library saves a small, visible sum and creates a large, scattered, invisible bill that someone else will pay later.

Then there is the question of what a library does for the mind, which is harder to put in a spreadsheet. Search engines are marvellous at answering the question you have already thought of. A library shelf is better at answering the question you did not know you had. You go in search of a book on Roman roads and your eye falls on one about medieval cookery, which you borrow on a whim, and three weeks later you are making a pie from a recipe seven centuries old. The algorithm that proposes your next purchase learns from what you have already bought; the shelf, being organised by subject and not by your history, can still surprise you.

A librarian, moreover, is among the last professionals whose role is to help without selling anything. In an age when so much of what we read has been filtered by commercial interests, the ability to ask a trained human being, "Where can I find reliable information about this?", is an underrated civic resource. Librarians do not tell us what to believe; they teach us to weigh sources, a skill that has never been more urgent.

The critics sometimes grant all this and then offer a compromise: let us keep a few central libraries and close the small branches. This, I think, misunderstands how libraries work. A library succeeds because it is near. The elderly man will not take two buses to a distant hub, and the teenager will not travel across town after school. Close the branch and you do not concentrate the service; you remove it from the very people who need it most.

I am not saying that libraries should resist change. The best of them have already transformed themselves, lending tools and musical instruments, hosting repair cafes and language classes, offering quiet rooms to freelancers and recording studios to teenagers. They have become community centres that happen to contain books, and I think that is a fine thing to be. The danger lies not in their evolution but in their neglect.

A society reveals what it values by what it refuses to charge for. We still, as a rule, allow people to walk through a park and drink from a public fountain, and to sit for a whole afternoon among a hundred thousand books without paying a penny. That seems to me one of the quiet triumphs of civilisation, and it would be an act of collective forgetfulness to give it away in order to save the price of a few flats.

questions.question: What do critics say about libraries?
questions.answer: That books are outdated, everything is online and the building costs too much.

questions.question: Why is the library unusual as a public space?
questions.answer: You are welcome without having to buy anything.

questions.question: Why does the writer say that 'everything is online' is not true for everyone?
questions.answer: Many people lack a connection, a device or confidence.

questions.question: Why should small branch libraries be kept?
questions.answer: Because libraries succeed when they are near people who need them.
